description: Technology Code on reusing existing platforms and services

args.question: What does the Technology Code say about reusing existing platforms and services?

review_criteria.relevance: Inspect the full question and returned section text, including every material topic; a heading alone is insufficient.
review_criteria.completeness: Record answered and unanswered parts; retrieval silence is not evidence no guidance exists.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":290,"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Searched for: technology, code, say, reusing, existing, platforms, services
How to cite: put the "Cite inline as" link in your sentence, straight after the point it supports. Do not add a sources or references list at the end.

## 1. Reuse as much as possible > Look at existing services
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2021-09-29, over three years ago: verify it is still current.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Look at existing services](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/making-services-in-an-emergency#look-at-existing-services))

Section text (verbatim):
> Before you start designing the service, look at existing government services with similar patterns or purposes. This will help you to:
> avoid creating something unnecessary if an existing service could be adapted
> find technology, design patterns and existing research that could be reused
> HMRC’s existing Making Tax Digital platform allowed them to create services very quickly as they could make use of existing patterns and technology.
> The Kickstart Scheme team at the Department for Work and Pensions designed a digital service to go live in one week by repurposing an existing service with similar patterns.

## 2. Reuse as much as possible > Reuse technology
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2021-09-29, over three years ago: verify it is still current.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Reuse technology](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/making-services-in-an-emergency#reuse-technology))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "Then, when the immediate crisis has passed and you have more time, revisit these decisions to see what you should change."

Section text (verbatim):
> Reuse technology as much as possible. You may need to make decisions about the short-term use of technology that are different from what you would do if you had more time. Keep a record of what decisions you have made due to time constraints. Then, when the immediate crisis has passed and you have more time, revisit these decisions to see what you should change.
> If you decide to use freely available technology, or you are offered a paid technology solution for free, be very careful that this does not lock you into using a specific supplier in future that may choose to charge. Have an exit plan and the ability to migrate to different technology. Get advice from GDS if you are unsure.
> Follow the guidelines for procurement in an emergency.

## 3. 8. Share, reuse and collaborate
Source: The Technology Code of Practice (`tcop`), Central Digital and Data Office. Authority: mandatory. page last updated 2025-07-07, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([The Technology Code of Practice: 8. Share, reuse and collaborate](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-technology-code-of-practice#share-reuse-and-collaborate))
**WARNING (SUPERSEDED, curated):** on spend control process, since 2026-04-01, this source is overtaken by "Getting approval to spend money on a service" (`spend-controls`). Treat the Service Manual as current on who approves digital spend. TCoP remains current on the technology standards themselves, only its spend control section is stale.

Section text (verbatim):
> Avoid duplicating effort and unnecessary costs by collaborating across government and sharing and reusing technology, data, and services.
> Read more about TCoP point 8 - Share, reuse and collaborate.

## 4. Common platforms and standards
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2024-09-03, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Common platforms and standards](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/using-common-components#common-platforms-and-standards))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [MANDATORY] "Any common platform you use must have been assured and found to produce outputs that meet the relevant government requirements."

Section text (verbatim):
> Any common platform you use must have been assured and found to produce outputs that meet the relevant government requirements.
> For example, only use a form building platform if it’s been assured and found to produce forms which meet the required standards for accessibility, security and compatibility with operating systems and browsers. But assuming it has, you will not need to:
> test the your service’s performance of individual forms
> test the frontend code of individual forms for accessibility
> test with assistive technologies
> get an accessibility audit
> test individual forms for compatibility with different browsers and devices
> carry out vulnerability and penetration testing on individual forms
> If you’re using a SaaS-type form building platform, you won’t need to consider hosting, deployment or monitoring uptime and performance - assuming that’s built into the platform.

## 5. Use infrastructure as code
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2024-10-24, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Use infrastructure as code](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/manage-your-software-configuration#use-infrastructure-as-code))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "When documenting technology components, you should include information on:"

Section text (verbatim):
> One way you can manage configuration is by using code to describe the configuration and software dependencies. Dependencies are the things your software needs in order to work properly.
> This approach brings all the advantages of programming in general and allows you to:
> test your code ability
> reuse your code
> document your infrastructure
> Once written in code, the infrastructure configuration is then run against the servers, networks and software in question.
> When documenting technology components, you should include information on:
> service vulnerabilities
> how you will assess the effectiveness of security controls
> who is responsible for ensuring asset security

## 6. 3. Context > 3.4 Technology
Source: Government Functional Standard GovS 005: Digital (`govs-005`), Government Digital Service. Authority: mandatory. page last updated 2026-10-01.
Cite inline as: ([Government Functional Standard GovS 005: Digital: 3.4 Technology](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital-html#technology))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "Organisations should select, buy, deploy and manage them safely, securely and responsibly, with clear lifecycle ownership, assurance, proportionate risk management and meaningful human control at the right stages."
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "Service Manual", pages about 5.3 years apart: "Organisations should have COVID-19 operating guidelines to minimise the risk to researchers." https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/doing-user-research-during-coronavirus-covid-19-choosing-face-to-face-or-remote-research#protecting-researchers
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "The Rose Book: guidance on knowledge asset management in government", pages about 2.5 years apart: "Organisations must comply with the law governing personal data and ensure data is treated safely, securely and ethically within appropriate governance frameworks." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/knowledge-asset-management-in-government/knowledge-asset-management-strategies-what-to-include-and-where-to-start#data-collection

Section text (verbatim):
> Technology means the systems, platforms, infrastructure, applications and tools used to deliver, run, secure and improve government services and organisational capabilities.
> This includes physical and cloud infrastructure, networks, end-user devices, hosting environments and other components used to create, process, store, secure and share information.
> This includes artificial intelligence technologies. Organisations should select, buy, deploy and manage them safely, securely and responsibly, with clear lifecycle ownership, assurance, proportionate risk management and meaningful human control at the right stages.
> Technology also includes software, applications, integrations, automation and code used to:
> provide interfaces for users, staff and other systems
> support policy delivery, operational processes, service management and decision making
